SEC13A-01.note: Two independent clauses; second has a noun-clause subject ('how the animals tell... remained uncertain'). ', but how' joins them. B comma splice; C '; though how' leaves a though-fragment after the semicolon; D 'in how' strips the second clause of its subject (glance-strikeable). Strongest distractor B, since the long noun-clause subject hides the splice. PHASE 2: Key A accepted; explanation correct (though as subordinator after semicolon -> fragment). Keep.

SEC13A-02.note: 'reveal [to anyone familiar only with the finished impressions] [how many... were cut]': the how-clause is the direct object, so no punctuation between the shifted indirect phrase and the object. A's comma is the strong distractor: the long fronted to-phrase invites a comma. C leaves reveal with no object and makes a how-fragment; D 'and how' coordinates nothing. PHASE 2: Key B accepted; explanation correct, including the 'and how' reading as second object of 'with'. Keep; one of the genuinely hard items.

SEC13A-03.note: No option ends the sentence, so the until-clause must open a second independent clause ('photographers... had to carry') and a coordinator is required: ', so until'. A comma splice (the strong distractor, since 'dried, until' reads naturally as a trailing until-clause); B same run-on; D 'even' is not a conjunction. 'so' logic holds (ten-minute window -> carry a darkroom). PHASE 2: Key C accepted; explanation correct. Keep; hard. Note topic duplicates SEC13B-03 (wet-plate photography, same ten-minute fact) - do not ship both in one form.

SEC13A-04.note: Interrupter opened by a dash after 'revealed' must close with a dash. Glancing back for the opening dash strikes A, B, C without parsing; length of the interrupter is the only difficulty. Strongest distractor A (comma, because of the inner comma pair). PHASE 2: Key D accepted; explanation correct. Recommend drop FOR THE HARD ROUTE only: dash-pair mirror is solvable by glancing back for the opening dash; all three distractors strike free. Fine as a medium item.

SEC13A-05.note: 'make one pattern unmistakable' is complete; the following independent clause specifies the pattern, so colon. A comma splice (strongest, because 'in nearly every season...' looks like a fronted phrase); C run-on; D 'which' has no gap to fill (strikeable). PHASE 2: Key B accepted. Minor wording slip: explanation calls the no-comma option C a 'comma splice' (it is a run-on/fused join; there is a comma after 'survives' but not at the clause boundary). Rule and path still produce the key. Keep.

SEC13A-06.note: 'Beside several of the deeper prints..., they identified...' is an independent clause; semicolon. A comma splice (strongest: 'beside' can read as attaching to the trackway); B fused; D 'beside which several... prints, they identified' leaves a broken relative. Requires locating 'they identified' far past the blank. PHASE 2: Key C accepted; explanation correct (same mild 'comma splice' label for B). Keep.

SEC13B-01.note: Subject 'The fossil teeth that... dug from an eroding riverbank over a single wet summer' runs into the verb 'settled'; no punctuation. A dash is the strongest distractor (echoes the closed dash pair before it) but opens an unclosed dash; C puts a lone comma inside subject; B 'which' turns the clause into a relative and leaves 'teeth' verbless. PHASE 2: Key D accepted; explanation correct. Keep.

SEC13B-02.note: Inverse of the usual however item: 'when researchers gave it to mice, whose livers... fragments' is subordinate, so the main clause is 'the antiviral effect... vanished' and 'however' sits as an interrupter between them: ', however,'. A (the textbook '; however,') is the strong distractor but strands the when-clause as a fragment after the earlier semicolon; B same fragment; D 'however;' fragment and odd (strikeable by surface). PHASE 2: Key C accepted; explanation correct. Keep; best item in the batch - inverts the trained '; however,' reflex.

SEC13B-03.note: Closing dash after 'poisoning' requires an opening dash: '—three chemicals...—'. Glance at the closing dash strikes A, C, D. Strongest distractor C (comma appositive) but mismatched marks. PHASE 2: Key B accepted; explanation correct. Drop for hard route: closing dash after 'poisoning' gives it away at a glance (easy). Also duplicates SEC13A-03's topic.

SEC13B-04.note: Direct question with inversion ('did they leave') and a question mark must be its own sentence: '. Why'. B comma splice of declarative + direct question is the strongest distractor; C fused; D 'asking why... did they' clashes with the inversion and question mark (strikeable). The question mark gives the item away. PHASE 2: Key A accepted; explanation correct. Drop for hard route: the question mark plus 'did they' inversion settles it without parsing; easy.

SEC13B-05.note: 'gathers' needs a subject; only 'protein that... rapidly gathers' supplies one. C and D leave 'in the presence... gathers' subjectless; B 'and' would make 'researchers' the subject of singular present 'gathers'. Strongest distractor D/C (fronted phrase looks like a sentence start). PHASE 2: Key A accepted; explanation correct. Keep.

SEC13B-06.note: Appositive 'a former apprentice... when he quit the workshop' opened by a comma after 'the printer' must close with a comma before the direct object 'the exclusive right'. B dash mismatches the opening comma; A period strands 'granted the printer...'; C no closure (strongest distractor, given the long embedded who-clause). PHASE 2: Key D accepted; explanation correct. Keep (medium).
